structure.overview: The Applicant, a Tamil citizen of Sri Lanka, seeks judicial review of the Refugee Appeal Division's (RAD) decision affirming the Refugee Protection Division's (RPD) finding that she is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection, based on the availability of an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Matara. The Applicant argued that the RAD erred in its assessment of the IFA test, misapplied Gender Guidelines, and misunderstood her personal circumstances, while the Respondent maintained the RAD's decision was reasonable. The Federal Court dismissed the judicial review application, finding the RAD's decision reasonable and refusing to certify the Applicant's proposed question for appeal.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant seeks judicial review of the RAD decision affirming the RPD's finding that she is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under the Act.
idea_list: RPD found Applicant not refugee or protected person

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27
citations.why: Defines refugee and protection criteria under the Act

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant is a Tamil citizen of Sri Lanka who lived in the UAE from 2011 to 2021; her husband still works there.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant owns paddy lands in Northern Sri Lanka and an apartment in Colombo.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In 2016, the Applicant rented out her lands and apartment; during the pandemic, she planned to return to Sri Lanka and end the tenancy, but the tenant demanded the lands.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant threatened eviction, and the tenant threatened to kill her and harm her children.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant gave up the paddy lands but the tenant remained in the apartment.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant confirmed the tenant's connection to the extremist group Bodu Bala Sena (BBS) in Sri Lanka.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant entered Canada on a visitor visa in December 2021 with her two Canadian-born children.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In December 2021, a friend told the Applicant that BBS members threatened him when checking on her apartment, warning him not to interfere.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant claimed refugee protection in Canada in January 2022.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RPD denied the Applicant's claim, including on the ground that an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) was available in Matara.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD considered the availability of the IFA as the determinative issue in the appeal.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant raises many arguments, but the court will only reference specific submissions as necessary.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent submits that the RAD made no reviewable errors in its decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Following Vavilov, the RAD's decision is reviewable on the reasonableness standard.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 653
citations.why: Establishes reasonableness as the standard of review for RAD decisions

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasonableness requires the decision to show justification, transparency, intelligibility, and be justified by relevant facts and law, per Vavilov para 99.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasonableness means the decision falls within a range of acceptable, defensible outcomes regarding facts and law, per Vavilov para 86.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The IFA test from Rasaratnam requires no serious possibility of persecution in the IFA and that it is reasonable to seek safety there before Canada.

citations.cite: Rasaratnam v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1992] 1 F.C. 706 at 710-711 (F.C.A.)
citations.why: Sets the two-part IFA test applied by the Board

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD misapprehended evidence, misunderstood her experience as a Tamil Hindu woman, and misapplied the first prong of the IFA test and Gender Guidelines.
idea_list: RAD misunderstood first prong of IFA test

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant complains the RAD unreasonably preferred its inferences over hers.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds no merit in the Applicant's argument about the RAD preferring its inferences over hers.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Huruglica confirms the RAD can review RPD decisions on correctness and draw its own inferences from evidence.

citations.cite: Huruglica v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2014] 4 F.C.R. 811 (F.C.)
citations.why: Confirms RAD's authority to review evidence and draw inferences

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD applied an excessive view for IFA and narrowly viewed her persecution as a Tamil Hindu female head of household without relatives.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues the RAD misapplied Gender Guidelines and that her education does not protect her from persecution.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant contends the RAD speculated about the tenant's motivation and improperly assessed her ability to end persecution by conceding the apartment, which is not part of the IFA test.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent argues the RAD made no reviewable errors and the decision was reasonable.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Applicant's claim is based on fear of harm from the tenant and BBS due to ethnicity, gender, and race as a Tamil Hindu woman.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RPD found a viable IFA in Matara, and the RAD confirmed this after independent review.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD addressed both parts of the IFA test and concluded the Applicant failed to show the tenant or BBS were motivated to find her in the IFA.

citations.why: Refers to the IFA test applied by the RAD

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD considered whether the tenant or BBS had means to locate the Applicant in the IFA, noting BBS government support but no guaranteed access to resources to find her.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD concluded the Applicant failed to prove the proposed IFA was unreasonable for her profile.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD noted the Applicant's husband supports her financially and she is well educated and able to work.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD confirmed a viable IFA is available to the Applicant.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues a section 96 claim should be decided before considering IFA, citing Thirunavukkarasu v. Canada (C.A.).

citations.cite: Thirunavukkarasu v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (C.A.), [1994] 1 F.C. 589
citations.why: Applicant relies on this case for section 96 claim order

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states refugee protection claims must be assessed before considering IFA; safe relocation negates refugee protection.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant alleges RAD erred by suggesting she give up apartment interest; the court rejects this, citing Malik v. Canada.
idea_list: Court rejects error citing Malik case

citations.cite: Malik v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 955
citations.why: Court relies on Malik to reject Applicant's error claim

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the RAD's finding on the apartment interest issue reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds no unreasonableness in RAD's application of Gender Guidelines and consideration of country conditions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with Respondent that RAD properly considered Applicant's personal circumstances and applied correct IFA test.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD reasonably assessed the first part of the IFA test regarding agents of persecution's motivation and means.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Although RAD found Applicant failed motivation part, it still considered whether agents had means to find her in IFA.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD reasonably concluded BBS lacks access to government documents to find Applicant in IFA, based on evidence.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD explained why threats to Applicant's friend do not prove ability to trace people countrywide.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD's decision meets the standard of review; judicial review application is dismissed.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant was given opportunity to submit proposed questions for certification.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant submitted a certification question about whether jeopardizing life is needed to prove IFA unreasonableness.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent opposed certification, citing FCA cases on certification criteria and why the question fails.
idea_list: Cites FCA cases on certification criteria

citations.cite: Lunyamila v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2018 FCA 22
Lewis v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2017 FCA 130, [2018] 2 F.C.R. 229
Lai v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2015 FCA 21, 29 Imm. L.R. (4th) 211
citations.why: Respondent cites for issue needing decision to certify

citations.cite: Mudrak v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FCA 178, 485 N.R. 186
citations.why: Respondent cites for question nature and facts

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant responded to the Respondent's submissions on certification by letter dated September 26, 2024.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court quotes subsection 74(d) of the Act on certification requirements for Federal Court of Appeal appeals.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with Respondent that the proposed question fails the certification test and has been addressed in prior decisions.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court refuses to certify the proposed question.
